sections.overview: The green sea turtle is a marine reptile of tropical and subtropical waters in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, and the Mediterranean. It is the largest hard-shelled sea turtle, moving through open-ocean juvenile habitat, coastal feeding grounds and sandy nesting beaches as it grows. Adults breathe air and migrate between feeding and breeding areas. The name “green” refers to the colour of some body fat, not the shell.
sections.identification: The smooth, oval carapace is usually brown, olive or mottled, above a pale plastron; hatchlings are dark above and pale below. A small rounded head, one pair of scales between the eyes and four pairs of costal scutes distinguish it from other hard-shelled sea turtles. Broad foreflippers provide propulsion, while hind flippers steer and help females dig nests. A typical adult has a straight carapace length near one metre and weighs about 150 kilograms, though sizes vary among populations. Mature males have longer tails and larger foreflipper claws than females.
sections.habitat: Adults and larger juveniles use shallow bays, lagoons and reef-fringed shores, especially where seagrass or algae are abundant. Hatchlings swim offshore and spend several years in open water, often among floating seaweed, before many settle into coastal feeding habitat; the timing varies among populations.
sections.diet: Diet changes with age: hatchlings and small oceanic juveniles take both animal and plant matter, while many older turtles graze algae and seagrass. Adults crop leaves with a keratin-covered beak and are predominantly herbivorous, though local menus vary. Microbes in the caecum and colon ferment fibrous plants, helping extract nutrients from bulky, low-energy food.
sections.behavior: In a St Croix study, juvenile green turtles usually foraged alone, though groups of up to three were seen. Biologgers on free-ranging juveniles in the Lesser Antilles recorded underwater rumbles during rest and grunts near other turtles; these sounds may serve social or warning roles, but their meanings remain untested. Experiments show that green turtles can use magnetic cues as a map for open-sea navigation.
sections.reproduction: Females mature late, often around 25–35 years, and adults return to breeding areas every few years. A female lays several clutches, commonly about two weeks apart, in sand chambers dug with her hind flippers; clutch size varies around a regional average near 100 eggs. Eggs incubate for roughly two months. Warmer nests tend to produce more females. Hatchlings emerge together and crawl toward the sea, where exhaustion and predators make their first journey dangerous.
sections.ecology: As a large herbivore, the green turtle links coastal plant production to marine food webs. Grazing trims seagrass and can create short, repeatedly cropped patches, sometimes encouraging fresh growth. Results depend on local plants and turtle density: a Great Barrier Reef experiment found an intense grazing patch at one site. Work in Lakshadweep documented seagrass decline under concentrated grazing, showing that turtle feeding can also damage habitat. Grazing can shape coastal habitats locally; turtles depend on their sustained productivity.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List now classifies the global species as Least Concern in 2025, replacing its 2004 global Endangered assessment. Regional populations remain uneven: the Central South Pacific is Endangered, the East Pacific and North Indian Ocean subpopulations are Vulnerable, and the Mediterranean Near Threatened. Overharvest of eggs, nesting females and feeding turtles, bycatch and habitat degradation have long reduced populations. Today, coastal development, vessel strikes, debris and disease remain pressures; hotter sand can skew hatchling sex ratios, while storms threaten nests. At southern Gulf of Mexico nesting sites, long-term protection and monitoring accompanied rising green turtle nest counts.
